abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are emerging as promising alternatives to traditional antibiotics, offering solutions to antimicrobial resistance through diverse mechanisms. Despite their potential, current computational approaches for AMP design rarely address strain-specific targeting, limiting their clinical efficacy as bacterial strains exhibit unique membrane compositions and susceptibility profiles requiring tailored interventions. Furthermore, the limited availability of strain-specific training data presents a significant challenge, necessitating parameter-efficient learning approaches that can optimize AMP properties with minimal overfitting. This study introduces a novel AMP generation framework that integrates reinforcement learning with a Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) model enhanced by Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) parameter-efficient fine-tuning. This approach enables the design of peptides optimized for multiple objectives, specifically antimicrobial activity and toxicity, tailored to individual pathogen strains. Our framework employs a two-stage learning process: pretraining on a large-scale peptide and AMP database to capture linguistic and contextual features, followed by reinforcement learning that leverages MIC (Minimum Inhibitory Concentration) and hemolysis prediction models to optimize antimicrobial potency and safety profiles. The integration of LoRA is crucial for efficiently adapting the model to strain-specific characteristics while addressing limited training data. The comparative analysis demonstrated our model’s superior performance over existing AMP generation approaches in both activity and hemolytic toxicity metrics. An ablation study confirmed the contributions of reinforcement learning and LoRA. Furthermore, the model can generate peptides satisfying both activity and toxicity conditions for unseen strains, highlighting its capability to design AMPs for emerging pathogens. In addition, molecular dynamics (MDs) simulations confirmed that the generated peptides penetrate bacterial membranes, supporting antimicrobial activity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The discovery of antibiotics between the 1940s and 1960s provided a major advancement in the treatment of bacterial infections and was widely used in food, agriculture, and various fields [1]. However, the overuse of antibiotics has facilitated the emergence of resistant bacterial strains, now recognized as a critical global health threat [2]. According to a WHO report, around 700 000 people died from drug-resistant infections in 2019, and this number is expected to rise from 10 to 20 million by 2050, potentially making it the top cause of death globally [1, 3]. This shows why we need to identify potential new candidates that can reduce antibiotic-resistant pathogens.

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides that play a crucial role in the host’s innate immune system. They respond to a wide range of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, parasites, and viruses. They significantly contribute to immune defense by targeting a broad spectrum of pathogens [4]. AMPs primarily inhibit microbial growth through diverse specialized mechanisms, often targeting cell membranes or specific intracellular components [5]. Despite their potential, the clinical application of naturally derived AMPs faces several challenges [6]. While efforts to identify and design clinically relevant AMPs have led to the discovery of over 2800 molecules, only a small fraction has advanced to preclinical studies, clinical trials, FDA approval, or commercialization. The primary reasons for the failure of the trials include the inability to achieve clinical efficacy targets, lack of improved activity compared to existing antibiotics, systemic and local toxicity, and high manufacturing costs. Therefore, the primary objective of biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies is to develop AMPs that are selective against pathogenic bacteria, exhibit safety for host cells, evade resistance development, and are cost-effective in production [7]. This highlights the critical importance of designing AMPs to reduce low efficacy, high toxicity, or cost [6].

Recent advances in deep generative models have driven the development of diverse approaches for designing AMPs. Generative models have been constructed based on foundational architectures like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) [8], Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [9], Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [10], and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [11]. Muller used an LSTM-based model [12] to generate new sequences by learning the structural patterns of helical AMPs [13]. Tucs et al. proposed PepGAN, a GAN-based model for generating AMPs. Through adversarial learning, the system improves its ability to produce effective peptides by distinguishing generated peptides from real ones [14]. Subsequently, conditional deep generative models have emerged as advanced tools for designing AMPs that satisfy specific criteria, such as enhanced antimicrobial efficacy, reduced toxicity, or defined structural characteristics. By leveraging input conditions, these models enable the generation of peptides with tailored properties, facilitating a more precise and efficient approach to AMP optimization. Szymczak et al. introduced HydrAMP [15], a conditional variational autoencoder that learns low-dimensional representations of peptides and captures their strong antimicrobial activities. Payel et al. developed PepCVAE [16], a peptide generation framework based on a semi-supervised VAE model that can design AMP sequences while also considering factors such as activity or toxicity. Additionally, PrefixProt [17] was proposed as a controllable protein design method, which uses virtual tokens as control tags through a prefix-tuning [18] approach for specific purposes such as alpha-helix structures, AMPs, or anticancer properties. Wang et al. introduced MoFormer [19], a deep learning model designed to optimize multiple properties simultaneously, enhancing antimicrobial activity while minimizing hemolytic effects.

Despite these advancements, several critical challenges remain unaddressed in current AMP design approaches. First, most existing AMP generation models focus on optimizing peptides for general antimicrobial properties without guaranteeing activity against specific target strains, significantly limiting clinical efficacy since bacterial strains exhibit unique membrane compositions and susceptibility profiles that demand tailored therapeutic interventions. Second, several recent AMP generation models have attempted to simultaneously optimize both antimicrobial activity and safety profiles such as hemolytic toxicity. MoFormer [19] employs a transformer architecture with multi-objective optimization and fused descriptors to design AMPs optimized for MIC and hemolysis against Escherichia coli. HMAMP [20] integrates GAN and reinforcement learning, maximizing hypervolume to achieve balanced optimization of MIC and hemolysis against E. coli. AMP-Designer [21], a GPT-based framework, combines knowledge distillation, and reinforcement learning to generate AMPs optimized for the same objectives. However, these approaches are typically limited to a small number of specific bacterial strains and fail to achieve multi-objective optimization across diverse strains. Moreover, existing methods that aim to cover multiple bacterial strains often require building and maintaining separate models for each strain, resulting in significant inefficiency and practical limitations. Third, the limited availability of strain-specific training data poses a substantial challenge, necessitating parameter-efficient learning approaches that can optimize AMP properties with minimal data requirements while avoiding overfitting, as traditional fine-tuning methods that update all model parameters are prone to overfitting when applied to small, strain-specific datasets.

To address these challenges, we propose AMP-RL, a novel framework designed to generate peptides that simultaneously satisfy both antimicrobial activity and non-hemolytic properties for individual bacterial strains. Our approach integrates three key innovations. First, a GPT-based model [22] is pretrained on peptide sequences and AMPs to capture essential biological and structural characteristics of AMPs. Second, we adopt reinforcement learning with objective-driven reward functions to optimize multiple competing objectives, specifically high antimicrobial activity and low hemolytic toxicity, in a strain-aware manner. Third, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [23] enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning that facilitates adaptation to individual target strains despite limited strain-specific data. This comprehensive framework not only addresses the challenges of strain-specific targeting and multi-objective optimization but also provides a flexible approach for generating AMPs tailored to specific bacterial pathogens, potentially accelerating the development of novel antimicrobial agents to combat the growing threat of antibiotic resistance.

sec.title: Datasets
sec.p: This study employs a three-stage training process: peptide pretraining, AMP pretraining, and reinforcement learning. In this section, we provide a detailed explanation of the data collection and processing used in the pretraining stages for peptides and AMPs.

Peptide Pretraining In the peptide pretraining stage, we extracted peptide sequences from the PeptideAtlas [24] database (accessed December 2024). This resulted in 1 725 301 unique peptides, of which 1 656 289 were used for training and 69 012 for validation.

AMP Pretraining In the AMP pretraining stage, we used the DBAASP v3 [25] database, which contains AMP sequences and MIC values for various bacterial strains. After manual curation, the dataset was divided into 7343 training, 918 validation, and 919 test samples, all derived from 35 bacterial strains used in AMP pretraining.

Additionally, 811 samples from the other 10 unseen strains were assigned to an external unseen set. This set was utilized to evaluate the model’s capacity for peptide generation in bacterial species that were not included in the training set.

The number of peptides used in peptide pretraining and AMP pretraining is presented in Table 1. Preprocessing details for peptide and AMP pretraining, along with detailed statistics for each bacterial strain, are summarized in Table S1 and Table S2 in the Supplementary Information.

sec.title: Overview of AMP-RL
sec.p: The AMP-RL framework consists of two main stages: pretraining and reinforcement learning (Fig. 1). In the pretraining stage (Fig. 1A), a large-scale peptide dataset, PeptideAtlas [24], is used to pretrain a language model to acquire general knowledge about peptide sequences. Subsequently, additional AMP data, DBAASP v3 [25], is collected and utilized to further fine-tune the pretrained language model, allowing it to specialize in AMP related knowledge. This process is designed to enable the model to generate potential AMP sequences effectively.

caption.p: The overall architecture of the AMP-RL framework for targeted antimicrobial peptide design. (A) Pretraining stage: Sequential training on PeptideAtlas [24] (general peptide dataset) followed by DBAASP v3 [25] (antimicrobial peptide dataset). (B) Reinforcement learning stage: The pretrained model is optimized through reinforcement learning guided by two predictors: a strain-specific MIC predictor and a hemolysis predictor. LoRA [23] enables parameter-efficient strain-specific training, while Experience memory prioritizes high-performing candidates. (C) Evaluation pipeline: Generated peptides undergo property prediction to assess antimicrobial activity and toxicity, structure prediction using DSSP [30] and AlphaFold3 [31], and molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate membrane interactions with bacterial cell membranes.

graphic.alt-text: A 3-stage diagram showing the overall architecture of the AMP-RL framework. (A) The pretraining stage, where the model is sequentially trained on PeptideAtlas and DBAASP v3. (B) The reinforcement learning stage, where the model is optimized using feedback from MIC and hemolysis predictors, utilizing LoRA and Experience Memory. (C) The evaluation pipeline stage, where generated peptides are validated through activity prediction, structure prediction, and MD simulations.

sec.p: The reinforcement learning stage (Fig. 1B) employs independent predictive models for antimicrobial activity (MIC) [26] and hemolytic toxicity [27] to guide the pretrained language model. These models direct the pretrained language model to generate AMP sequences with high antimicrobial activity and low hemolytic toxicity through reinforcement learning. Here, MIC refers to the minimum concentration of an antibiotic required to inhibit microbial growth, with lower MIC values indicating higher potency at lower concentrations [28]. Hemolysis refers to the destruction of red blood cells caused by peptides, leading to premature cell rupture and reduced lifespan, which poses a significant side effect limiting their therapeutic potential [29]. The training process is designed to optimize AMP generation by reducing MIC values while minimizing hemolytic toxicity.

To further enhance efficiency, LoRA [23] was introduced, allowing for parameter-efficient training and enabling the generation of strain-specific AMPs. This approach ensures effective AMP generation even in limited data environments by updating only a small subset of model parameters while preserving the foundational knowledge learned during pretraining. The resulting framework provides a structured and scalable approach for systematic AMP design and optimization i.e. computationally efficient for practical application in standard research environments (see details in Table S3 in the Supplementary Information).

For evaluation (Fig. 1C), we assessed whether the generated peptides met both MIC and non-hemolytic conditions for each strain. Following a filtering process, structure prediction and molecular dynamics (MDs) simulation were performed to examine the structural properties and potential effectiveness of the generated peptides.

sec.title: Pretraining
sec.p: We employed the GPT architecture based on the GPT-2 [22] base model for our generative model. Our AMP-RL model consists of 12 Transformer decoder layers and 12 attention heads, with a hidden dimension of 768. Pretraining was conducted sequentially using the PeptideAtlas [24] and DBAASP v3 [25] databases (Table 1), allowing the model to gradually learn knowledge about general peptides and then specifically about AMPs. For sequence generation, we adopted Causal Language Modeling (CLM), where the model predicts the next token based on the previously generated sequence. This approach enables the model to learn the sequential characteristics of peptide data. Further details are available in the Pretraining section in the Supplementary Information.

sec.title: Low-rank adaptation
sec.p: We applied the LoRA technique to train models for each bacterial strain in a parameter-efficient manner. LoRA freezes the pretrained model’s weights and adds trainable low-rank matrices into the query, key, value, and output layers, significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters.

By leveraging LoRA, we adopted a strain-aware weight-swapping mechanism within a single AMP-RL model instead of training separate models. This enabled flexible adaptation to different strains while maintaining memory efficiency. The approach is particularly effective given the limited amount of training data available.
To ensure stable learning and valid sequence generation, LoRA weights were integrated during the pretraining phase, not only during reinforcement learning.

As a result, the LoRA-based AMP-RL model enables more flexible strain-aware weight adaptation, reduces memory consumption, and provides an optimized approach that enhances training efficiency. Further details are available in the LoRA section in the Supplementary Information.

sec.title: Reinforcement learning
sec.p: We applied RL for fine-tuning, enabling the generation of AMPs with low MIC and nonhemolytic properties for each bacterial strain.

In each iteration, 2000 new sequences were generated and evaluated using HemoDL [27] and LLAMP [26]. Additionally, 1000 sequences were sampled from an Experience memory (buffer size: 5000), which stored peptides sorted by MIC score first, followed by sorting based on hemolysis score. When the buffer reached its capacity, the top sequences were retained to match the buffer size. The resulting batch of 3000 peptides was then used to calculate rewards and update the policy using the REINFORCE algorithm [32] to maximize expected rewards. This process was repeated across all eight strains.

sec.title: Evaluation of training effectiveness and generative quality
sec.p: For pretraining, we evaluated model performance using perplexity. The perplexity decreased from 15.0 to 13.4 in peptide pretraining, and from 9.1 to 4.6 in AMP pretraining, indicating effective learning. For reinforcement learning, we measured the average reward per iteration for MIC and hemolysis. Rewards increased over time, indicating effective optimization. These results are shown in Supplementary Information Fig. S1. To analyze how the model balances the two objectives of antibacterial activity and non-hemolytic toxicity during reinforcement learning, we compared models trained with and without the Experience memory mechanism. Supplementary Information Fig. S2 presents the reward trajectories for both settings, clearly demonstrating the role of Experience memory in promoting balanced optimization across the two objectives. We also evaluated the quality of peptides generated after reinforcement learning by comparing diversity, uniqueness, and novelty across AMP-RL and baseline models. The results demonstrate that AMP-RL achieves comparable diversity, uniqueness, and novelty to the baseline models. These results, along with additional analyses, are provided in Supplementary Information Tables S5–S12.

sec.title: Strain-aware property analysis
sec.p: To investigate the functional characteristics of strain-aware AMPs generated by AMP-RL, we first analyzed their amino acid composition and physicochemical properties compared to non-strain-specific AMPs. Non-strain-specific AMPs encompass sequences that demonstrate activity against diverse bacterial targets without strain-specific optimization, serving as a baseline for comparison with our strain-optimized generated peptides. For each strain, we generated 1000 peptides using the trained AMP-RL model.

As shown in Figs 2A–H, peptides generated for different Gram-type bacterial strains exhibited distinct amino acid composition profiles. To enable more biologically meaningful comparisons, we conducted separate comparative analyses using Gram-type specific background datasets rather than a single universal comparison set. We divided the DBAASP v3 database into Gram-positive and Gram-negative specific subsets based on the bacterial targets of each AMP, then used these subsets as appropriate background datasets for comparing peptides generated for each strain type.

caption.p: Analysis of amino acid composition and physicochemical properties. (A–H) comparison of amino acid compositions between peptides generated for each strain (blue) and known AMPs from the DBAASP v3 database (orange). P-values result from the hypergeometric test (*: P < .05, **: P < .01, ***: P < .001). (I–N) violin plots of six physicochemical properties. Properties were calculated and compared across peptides generated for each strain, peptides from the PeptideAtlas and DBAASP v3 databases, and peptides generated by the prior model.

graphic.alt-text: A collection of charts analyzing amino acid composition and physicochemical properties. (A-H) are bar graphs comparing amino acid compositions of generated peptides (blue) versus DBAASP v3 AMPs (orange). (I-N) are violin plots comparing six physicochemical properties across multiple groups, including generated peptides, PeptideAtlas, and DBAASP v3.

sec.p: Our Gram-type specific analysis revealed distinct optimization patterns that support our model’s strain-aware capabilities. For Gram-positive bacterial strains, the generated peptides showed significantly increased proportions of cysteine (C), proline (P), arginine (R), and tryptophan (W) compared to known Gram-positive active sequences from the database. For Gram-negative bacterial strains, the generated peptides exhibited elevated levels of cysteine (C), proline (P), arginine (R), and tyrosine (Y) compared to known Gram-negative active sequences. These amino acid enrichment patterns carry important biological significance for AMP design. Proline residues are frequently found in proline-rich AMPs and often form repetitive motifs with arginine (R), which are known for selective activity against Gram-negative bacteria while maintaining low mammalian toxicity [33]. The combination of arginine and tryptophan residues in high proportions has been associated with potent antimicrobial activity and broad antimicrobial spectrum coverage [34]. Furthermore, proline inclusion in peptide sequences has been consistently associated with significantly reduced hemolytic activity compared to proline-free analogs [35–37], supporting our dual optimization objective.

These findings demonstrate that our model successfully learns to incorporate specific amino acid residues that enhance antimicrobial activity while simultaneously reducing toxicity, providing strong evidence for effective strain-aware optimization that goes beyond simply replicating general AMP characteristics.

Physicochemical property analysis revealed comprehensive optimization patterns in AMP-RL-generated peptides (Figs 2I–N). Our generated peptides maintained appropriate length distributions (Fig. 2I) while exhibiting significantly enhanced cationic characteristics compared to randomly extracted PeptideAtlas sequences, particularly in charge-to-length ratio (CTLR) (Fig. 2J) and cationic charged residue content (Fig. 2K), demonstrating that our model consistently generates peptides with enhanced positive charge characteristics across all bacterial strains compared to both random PeptideAtlas sequences and our GPT prior model. This enhanced cationic character is crucial because positive charge enables essential electrostatic binding interactions with negatively charged bacterial membrane components.

The aliphatic index values (Fig. 2L) indicated an optimal balance between peptide stability and membrane interaction capability. Critically, generated peptides preserved essential amphipathic properties as measured by hydrophobic moment (Fig. 2M) and maintained appropriate hydrophobic residue ratios (Fig. 2N) that closely resembled validated AMPs from the DBAASP v3 database.

These findings confirm that AMP-RL effectively captured intrinsic AMP characteristics while introducing strain-aware optimizations that enhance key functional properties without compromising essential physicochemical foundations. Statistical test details are provided in Fig. S3 in the Supplementary Information.

sec.title: Reinforcement learning performance analysis
sec.p: To evaluate the multi-objective optimization performance of the AMP-RL model, we generated 1000 peptides using AMP-RL and five state-of-the-art AMP generation models (PepCVAE [16], HydrAMP [15], PrefixProt [17], TG-CDDPM [38], and AMP Designer [21]), and assessed their ability to meet MIC and hemolysis objectives.

MIC values were predicted using a Random forest [39] model, additionally built and trained on the AMP pretraining dataset, while hemolytic activity was evaluated using HemoPred [40], a web-based prediction model. Detailed information on these predictive models is provided in Fig. S4, Table S13, and Table S14 in the Supplementary Information. The evaluation of each comparison model was conducted using peptide sequences that were directly generated by the original authors of each respective model.

Figure 3A shows the average non-hemolysis probability (x-axis, from HemoPred [40]) and normalized MIC value (y-axis, scaled using Equation S5 in the Supplementary Information) per model. Higher values in both axes indicate peptides with better antimicrobial activity and lower toxicity. AMP-RL outperformed the baseline models in each objective, namely antimicrobial activity and hemolytic toxicity. To further understand performance on each individual objective, Fig. 3B presents the proportion of non-hemolytic peptides among the 1000 peptides generated by each model. AMP-RL achieved a non-hemolytic rate of 65.4%, outperforming all baseline models, including TG-CDDPM (58.2%), the previous best-performing model. In contrast, PrefixProt [17], which showed strong MIC performance, exhibited the lowest non-hemolytic rate (32.2%), highlighting a trade-off between antimicrobial activity and toxicity.

caption.p: (A) Comparison of mean non-hemolysis probability (x-axis) and normalized MIC value (y-axis) for each model. (B and C) Performance of predicted peptide proportions with non-hemolytic properties across models and strain, (D–K) comparison of MIC density distributions across models and strain, (L) performance of predicted peptide proportions with MIC ≤10uM and non-hemolytic properties across models and strain.

graphic.alt-text: A collection of charts evaluating model performance on antimicrobial activity and toxicity. (A) is a scatter plot comparing models, with mean non-hemolysis probability and normalized MIC value as axes. (B and C, L) are charts comparing the proportion of non-toxic and/or high-activity peptides by model. (D–K) shows a comparison of the proportion of peptides that are both high-activity and non-toxic, across models and strains.

sec.p: Figure 3C shows the strain-wise non-hemolytic rate of peptides generated by AMP-RL. Among eight bacterial strains, five exhibited a non-hemolytic rate above 60%, indicating AMP-RL’s consistent non-toxic performance across different strains.

Figures 3D–K shows the MIC density distribution per strain for each model. AMP-RL generated the highest proportion of peptides with low MIC values across all strains, with particularly strong performance against Acinetobacter baumannii and E. Coli. Since all comparison models except PepCVAE were also trained on the DBAASP dataset, evaluation using a MIC predictor trained based on the DBAASP database enables a fair comparison. (see Table S15 available online at http://bib.Oxfordjournals.Org/ in the Supplementary Information for details).

In addition, antimicrobial activity of the generated peptides was evaluated using the AMP classifier provided by CAMP [41]. The results showed that AMP-RL produced peptides with antimicrobial properties at levels comparable to those of baseline models. Strain-wise analysis showed consistent results, with AMP-RL generating peptides with AMP characteristics comparable to those from other models. (see Fig. S5 in the Supplementary Information for details).

We evaluated the ability of AMP-RL and baseline models to generate peptides that satisfy both antimicrobial activity and non-hemolytic properties. For this, 1000 peptides were generated per model, and the proportion meeting both criteria was analyzed.

Figure 3L presents the MIC and hemolysis prediction results for peptides generated by the baseline models and AMP-RL in a stacked bar format. MIC predictions were made using the random forest MIC prediction model described in Figs 3D–K, while hemolysis predictions were conducted using HemoPred [40], the hemolysis classification model employed in Fig. 3B and C. The proportion of peptides satisfying both conditions (MIC ≤10 μM and nonhemolytic properties) was then calculated and compared across models.

Figure 3L presents stacked bar plots of peptides predicted to meet both MIC (≤10 μM) and non-hemolytic criteria. The MIC threshold was set at 10 μM, in accordance with the positive peptide definition used in HydrAMP [15]. MIC was predicted using the same random forest model as in Figs 3D–K, and hemolysis was predicted using HemoPred [40]. AMP-RL peptides were generated 10 times with different seeds to assess consistency, with average counts and standard deviations reported. For each model, if fewer than 50 peptides satisfied both criteria for a given strain, the corresponding result was excluded from the figure.

As shown in Fig. 3L, AMP-RL consistently produced more peptides satisfying both conditions than all baseline models. For example, it generated 604 peptides for Bacillus subtilis, 154 more than TG-CDDPM [38], and 504 for E. coli, 228 more than TG-CDDPM. These results confirm that AMP-RL can effectively generate strain-aware AMPs that are both potent and low in toxicity.

This capability stems from the application of reinforcement learning, which enables the model to optimize for both antimicrobial activity and low toxicity simultaneously. Additionally, the use of strain-specific LoRA weights allows the model to adaptively generate peptides tailored to each bacterial strain. Ablation studies demonstrating the contributions of reinforcement learning and strain-specific LoRA are presented in Table S16 and Table S17, respectively, which can be found in the Supplementary Information.

sec.title: Unseen strain generation performance
sec.p: To assess AMP-RL’s generalization capability, we evaluated its performance on unseen bacterial strains (Streptococcus sanguinis and Pseudomonas putida). During the reinforcement learning stage, we employed an MIC predictor (LLAMP model) that was not trained on the unseen species to prevent the model from indirectly acquiring information about those species. To ensure a fair evaluation of the generated peptides, we additionally retrained the Random forest model using data from all 45 strains, including 10 unseen strains. This design ensures a strict separation between training and evaluation, thereby eliminating data leakage and maintaining the integrity of the generalization assessment. The predictive performance of the retrained model on the unseen strains is provided in Table S14 of the Supplementary information. This evaluation is crucial for determining whether our model can effectively design AMPs for emerging pathogens without requiring any retraining of the predictor.

We generated 1000 peptides using the trained model for each strain and compared their physicochemical property distributions with 1000 randomly sampled peptides from the DBAASP v3 [25] database (Fig. 4). Following the same approach as Fig. 2, we calculated key physicochemical properties, including CTLR, Aliphatic Index, Hydrophobic Moment, Cationic Charged Residue, and Hydrophobic Residue of the generated peptides.

caption.p: Analysis of physicochemical properties in peptides generated for unseen strains compared to reference datasets. (A–F) Violin plots of six physicochemical properties. Properties were calculated and compared across peptides generated for each unseen strain (S. sanguinis and P. putida), peptides from the PeptideAtlas [24] and DBAASP v3 [25] databases, and sequences generated by the prior model.

graphic.alt-text: A collection of six violin plots (A-F) comparing the physicochemical properties of peptides generated for unseen strains. Peptides for S. sanguinis and P. putida are compared against reference datasets, including PeptideAtlas, DBAASP v3, and a prior model.

sec.p: The analysis revealed that peptides generated for the two unseen strains exhibited distinctly different physicochemical property distributions compared to random peptides from the PeptideAtlas [24] database, particularly in CTLR and hydrophobic moment. Importantly, the generated peptides closely aligned with the physicochemical property distributions observed in the DBAASP v3 [25] database, which contains validated AMPs. This finding indicates that the model is not merely generating random peptide sequences but has been effectively trained to produce peptides with antimicrobial properties. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the model is capable of retaining physicochemical properties associated with antimicrobial activity even when generating peptides for unseen strains.

Figure 5 compares the proportion of peptides satisfying both MIC ≤10 μM and non-hemolytic conditions for unseen strains across different models. Results demonstrate that AMP-RL significantly outperformed all baseline models, generating 52.7% and 49% of peptides meeting both criteria for S. sanguinis and P. putida, respectively. Compared to the TG-CDDPM model [38], AMP-RL demonstrated improvements of 24.4% for S. sanguinis and 29.9% for P. putida. These findings suggest that AMP-RL is capable of robustly generating peptides with high antimicrobial activity and low toxicity, even in response to newly emerging bacterial strains.

caption.p: Performance comparison of peptide generation models for unseen strains, showing the proportion of generated peptides with MIC ≤10 μM and non-hemolytic properties: (left) S. sanguinis, (right) P. putida. The values in parentheses represent the standard deviation (SD) of the results obtained from 10 repeated experiments.

graphic.alt-text: Two bar charts comparing model performance for unseen strains: S. sanguinis (Left) and P. putida (Right). The charts plot the proportion of peptides with high activity (MIC ≤10 μM) and non-hemolytic properties. For both strains, the AMP-RL model shows a significantly higher proportion of effective peptides compared to other models.

sec.p: Furthermore, consistent high performance was observed in evaluations on completely unseen strains, such as S. sanguinis and P. putida. Critically, the MIC predictor used during reinforcement learning was trained exclusively on data from 35 species, excluding these unseen strains, while the evaluation was conducted using a separate model retrained on all 45 species, including the previously unseen ones. This strict separation ensures no data leakage between training and evaluation phases for these species, providing robust evidence that the model’s superior performance reflects genuine generalization capabilities rather than memorization of training data.

sec.title: Embedding analysis and visualization
sec.p: To gain deeper insights into the distribution patterns of our generated peptides in relation to known antimicrobial and hemolytic peptides, we conducted a t-SNE analysis based on embeddings derived from the ESM-2 [42] model, which was pretrained on 1.7 million peptide sequences from the PeptideAtlas dataset [24] (Fig. 6).

caption.p: Visualization of generated peptides in the embedding space. (A) t-SNE visualization of generated peptides with AMP contour distributions, (B) t-SNE visualization of generated peptides with hemolytic contour distributions.

graphic.alt-text: Two t-SNE visualizations (A and B) showing the distribution of generated peptides in an embedding space. (A) displays the peptides concentrated within high antimicrobial (AMP) probability contours. (B) displays the same peptides concentrated within low hemolytic (toxicity) probability contours.

sec.p: In Fig. 6A, the blue contour plot represents the embedding distribution of 1000 randomly sampled peptides from the DBAASP v3 [25] database. In Fig. 6B, the gray contour plot corresponds to 1000 randomly sampled peptides from the Hemolytik [43] database that are known to exhibit hemolytic properties. The red scatter plot depicts the embedding distribution of peptides generated for Gram-positive bacterial strains (B. subtilis, Enterococcus faecalis, S. aureus), where 1000 peptides were evenly sampled across the three strains. Similarly, the orange scatter plot represents the embedding distribution of peptides generated for Gram-negative bacterial strains (A. baumannii, E. coli, Enterobacter cloacae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa), following the same sampling strategy.

As shown in Fig. 6, the majority of peptides generated by AMP-RL cluster within the blue contour regions, indicating substantial similarity to known AMPs in the embedding space. Additionally, the majority of generated peptides avoid the high-density regions of the gray contour plot, suggesting that they predominantly exhibit non-hemolytic properties.

Furthermore, the scatter plot reveals a degree of separation between Gram-positive and Gram-negative peptides, indicating that the generated peptides reflect differences in bacterial strain characteristics in the embedding space. These findings demonstrate that the AMP-RL model not only generates peptides that satisfy antimicrobial and non-hemolytic conditions but also effectively captures strain-aware characteristics.

sec.title: Structure prediction and analysis of generated peptides
sec.p: To investigate the structural characteristics of the generated peptides, we employed the DSSP (Define Secondary Structure of Proteins) [30] for secondary structure prediction and AlphaFold3 [31] for 3D structure modeling. For structure prediction, we implemented a rigorous filtering process to select high-quality candidates. Peptides generated for each strain that met both MIC ≤10 μM and non-hemolytic criteria were prioritized. To ensure structural and sequence diversity, peptides with more than 80% sequence similarity were eliminated. Additionally, we excluded peptides with charge values below 4, instability indices exceeding 40, and sequence lengths greater than 30.

For the secondary structure analysis, we selected the top 20 potent peptides of each strain from the previous filtering outcome. The result revealed that peptides generated for different bacterial strains predominantly adopted α-helix conformations (Fig. S6). The α-helix structure, characterized by amphipathicity with distinct hydrophilic and hydrophobic faces, enables effective bacterial membrane interaction [35, 44]. This structural feature is particularly advantageous for antimicrobial activity as it facilitates membrane disruption through the insertion of the hydrophobic face into the lipid bilayer while maintaining electrostatic interactions between the hydrophilic face and the negatively charged bacterial membrane (see details in Fig. S6 and Fig. S7 of the Supplementary Information).

To predict and analyze the 3D structures of the peptides generated for each strain, we performed structure prediction using the AlphaFold3 model [31] with the top three potent peptides of each strain.

As shown in Fig. 7 and Fig. S7, most of the generated peptides predominantly adopted an α-helix structure, consistent with our secondary structure analysis. In addition to α-helical structures, some peptides exhibited mixed structures and coil conformations. This indicates that the model is not biased toward a specific secondary structure but is capable of generating peptides with diverse structural characteristics. These findings suggest that the AMP-RL model does not favor a particular structure but instead effectively designs strain-specific peptides by incorporating a variety of structural features.

caption.p: Predicted 3D structures of top-performing peptides for each bacterial strain using AlphaFold3. For each strain, the three peptides with the lowest predicted MIC values that also satisfy non-hemolytic criteria are shown.

graphic.alt-text: A collection of 3D peptide structures predicted by AlphaFold3. For each bacterial strain, such as E. coli and S. aureus, the 3D structures of the top 3 peptides satisfying the lowest MIC (high activity) and non-hemolytic (low toxicity) criteria are visualized.

sec.title: Molecular dynamics simulation
sec.p: To investigate the interaction capabilities between the peptides generated by AMP-RL and the bacterial cell membrane, MDs simulations were conducted.

For this analysis, we selected E. coli as a representative gram-negative strain and S. aureus as a representative gram-positive strain. From the previously filtered peptides, we chose the top three candidates with the lowest predicted MIC values that also satisfied our non-hemolytic criteria. Among these, we selected the peptide with the highest hydrophobic moment for simulation (the top 2 peptides shown in Fig. 7), as this property is critical for membrane interaction. The 3D structure of the selected peptide was predicted using the AlphaFold2 [45] model, and MD simulations were performed based on the predicted structure.

For bacterial membrane modeling, a web-based tool called CHARMM-GUI [46] was used. The molecular composition was set to a POPE/POPG/TOCL ratio of 7:2:1 for Gram-negative bacteria membrane and a POPG/POPE/DOTAP/TOCL ratio of 6:1.5:1.5:1 for Gram-positive bacteria membrane [38]. The force field, temperature, and other simulation conditions were automatically generated without any manual adjustment.
To quantify membrane interaction tendencies, we analyzed mass density distributions across the simulation trajectory, dividing it into three time intervals: 0–25 ns, 25–75 ns, and 75–100 ns.

As shown in Fig. 8A and B, the peptide increasingly interacts with the membrane over time, showing a gradual insertion into the membrane interface. These results suggest a strong interaction between the peptide and the bacterial membrane.

Mass density plots of the peptide and bacterial membrane over three simulation intervals: (left) 0–25 ns, (middle) 25–75 ns, and (right) 75–100 ns. (A) Shows results for E. coli, and (B) for S. aureus. The x-axis represents the position relative to the center of the membrane, while the y-axis indicates the mass density. The green curve represents the bacterial membrane, while the blue curve shows the peptide’s position relative to the membrane. VMD visualization of peptide–membrane interaction: (C) E. coli at 0 ns, (D) E. coli at 100 ns, (E) S. aureus at 0 ns, (F) S. aureus at 100 ns.

(A) and (B) are mass density plots for the peptide (blue) and bacterial membrane (green) across three-time intervals (0–25, 25–75, 75–100 ns). (C) through (F) are 3D visualizations of the peptide-membrane interaction at 0 ns and 100 ns.

sec.p: To further visualize these interactions, we employed the VMD tool [47] to observe the peptide’s membrane-associating behavior. Figs 8C–F display snapshots from the simulation at 0 ns and 100 ns, respectively (see details in Fig. S8 of the Supplementary Information). These visualizations also confirm that the peptide remains embedded in one leaflet of the gram-negative bacterial membrane. This observation is consistent with the trends seen in the mass density plots (Fig. 8A and B).

Overall, these analyses demonstrate that the peptides generated by AMP-RL effectively interact with E. coli and S. aureus membranes, exhibiting strong binding and membrane insertion. This indicates that AMP-RL is capable of generating peptides with structures favorable for antimicrobial activity.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, we present AMP-RL, a novel reinforcement learning-based framework for designing strain-specific de novo AMPs that optimize and balance potent antimicrobial activity with low hemolytic toxicity. Our approach integrates a GPT with LoRA to efficiently generate peptides optimized for specific bacterial strains while maintaining critical safety profiles.

Comparative evaluation against state-of-the-art models demonstrated AMP-RL’s superior performance in generating peptides that simultaneously satisfy both low MIC and nonhemolytic criteria. For key pathogens like B. subtilis and E. coli, AMP-RL produced substantially more viable candidates than existing methods. Significantly, this performance advantage extended to previously unseen bacterial strains, highlighting the model’s potential for addressing emerging pathogens without requiring additional training.

Structural analysis revealed that AMP-RL generates peptides with diverse structural characteristics, predominantly α-helical conformations but also including mixed and extended structures. This structural diversity reflects the model’s ability to optimize peptide architecture according to strain-specific requirements rather than defaulting to a single structural motif. Also, MDs simulations provided further validation of the functional potential of our generated peptides, demonstrating their ability to effectively interact with and penetrate bacterial membranes over time. This membrane-penetrating capability aligns with known mechanisms of action for effective AMPs.
However, a limitation of this study is the non-trivial overlap between the training and evaluation datasets used by the MIC and hemolysis predictors.

Regarding MIC prediction, identical datasets were used to train both the predictor utilized during the training phase and the one applied for evaluation purposes. For hemolysis prediction, while distinct models were employed for training versus evaluation, there is some dataset overlap, specifically with the HemoPI-2 [48] and HemoPI-3 [48] datasets (See Table S18 in the Supplementary Information for details on the dataset distribution). Such data overlap could potentially undermine evaluation objectivity, which we recognize as a study limitation. Nevertheless, given that all comparison baseline models, with the exception of PepCVAE, were trained using the same underlying dataset, employing a MIC predictor developed from the DBAASP database ensures equitable comparison conditions.

Importantly, when evaluating unseen bacterial strains, all predictors employed during both training and evaluation phases had no prior exposure to data from these species, ensuring unbiased comparison for these particular scenarios. As additional MIC and hemolysis datasets become accessible in the future, we intend to implement fully independent datasets for training and evaluation phases. This approach will enable more robust and statistically sound model performance comparisons.

Despite these limitations, these findings establish AMP-RL as a powerful framework for rational AMP design that addresses key challenges in the field: strain specificity, activity optimization, and toxicity minimization. By enabling targeted design of peptides with optimized properties, our approach opens new avenues for developing antimicrobial agents to combat the growing threat of antibiotic resistance.

Additionally, while this study establishes a computational generative framework for AMP discovery, experimental validation represents a crucial future direction to confirm the biological efficacy and safety of generated candidates. Such validation through laboratory collaborations will provide empirical evidence for the practical applicability of our computational predictions.

list-item.p: AMP-RL is a framework that efficiently generates antimicrobial peptides exhibiting potent activity across individual species while maintaining low hemolytic toxicity.
AMP-RL leverages reinforcement learning to generate peptides satisfying desired conditions, while using LoRA for species-adaptive, parameter-efficient model tuning.
Embedding visualization indicates that the generated peptides exhibit property-aligned distributions in the embedding space, and molecular dynamics simulations confirm their membrane permeability.
